qs.q: A 28-year-old woman with severe aplastic anemia shows no clinical improvement after completing a standard course of antithymocyte globulin and ciclosporin. Which therapeutic agent is most appropriate at this stage?
qs.e: Alemtuzumab is typically reserved as a rescue therapy for patients with aplastic anemia whose disease has failed initial immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin. Cyclophosphamide is generally used upfront rather than sequentially after failure.

qs.q: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and macrocytic anemia. A bone marrow biopsy is performed to differentiate myelodysplastic syndrome from aplastic anemia. Which finding is expected in myelodysplastic syndrome?
qs.e: Hypercellular bone marrow with effective hematopoiesis distinguishes myelodysplastic syndrome from aplastic anemia. Marrow showing no fibrosis is not specific for distinguishing these two conditions.

qs.q: Which of the following inherited syndromes featuring macrocytic cells is classified as a congenital aplastic anemia?
qs.e: Acquired and congenital aplastic anemias include Diamond-Blackfan and Fanconi syndromes, which present as macrocytic anemias with low or normal reticulocyte counts. Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II presents as a normocytic anemia.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Aplastic anemia is a bone‑marrow failure where all cell lines drop, causing pancytopenia. It presents with fatigue, bruising, and frequent infections. Early recognition and supportive care are lifesaving.

sections.p: Aplastic anemia is a hypocellular marrow with fatty infiltration and reduced hematopoiesis. Diagnosis requires a peripheral smear showing pancytopenia, a bone‑marrow aspirate with <5% cellularity, and exclusion of other causes.

t.b: Shows low RBC, WBC, platelets; helps rule out hemolysis
Confirms hypocellularity, fat infiltration, no dysplasia
Excludes iron overload; high levels suggest transfusion history

t.a: Viral serology (HIV, HBV, HCV, EBV, CMV)

sections.p: Severity is staged by the WHO criteria, using absolute neutrophil count, platelet count, and hemoglobin. Stages range from mild (low platelets) to severe (ANC <500).
b: WHO 2016: Grade 1–4 based on ANC, platelets, Hb

sections.p: Idiopathic is common; other causes include drug toxicity, viral infections, and environmental toxins. In low‑resource settings, infections and herbal remedies are frequent culprits.
Patients feel tired, bruise easily, and have frequent infections. Oral ulcers, petechiae, and bleeding gums are common. Fever may indicate infection.
Key tests confirm pancytopenia, rule out other causes, and assess marrow status. When tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and basic CBC guide management.

t.b: Detects pancytopenia; low ANC signals infection risk
Confirms hypocellularity; rules out dysplasia or leukemia

sections.p: Severe bleeding, septic shock, and uncontrolled infections are life‑threatening. Rapid drop in platelets or neutrophils warrants urgent care.
b: Signs of sepsis: fever, tachycardia, hypotension

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Supportive care includes transfusions, antibiotics, and growth factors. Immunosuppression (ATG + cyclosporine) is standard for severe cases.
b: Administer broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected
Use ATG + cyclosporine for severe AA

sections.p: Regular CBCs monitor response. Vaccinations against pneumococcus and influenza reduce infection risk. Avoid known marrow‑toxic drugs and herbal remedies.
Hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndrome, leukemia, and nutritional deficiencies can mimic aplastic anemia.
Early marrow changes may be subtle; a normal ferritin can mask iron overload from transfusions. Viral serology may be negative early.
